_readme: THE CEILINGS REGISTER — [pipeline B-6] company/pipeline/04-backend-platform.md
Every free-tier ceiling this portfolio runs against, recorded ONCE, each with the URL it was read
from and the date it was read. Every hard cap in the Worker source DERIVES from a row here.
WHY IT EXISTS. B-6's original acceptance criterion was 'a ceilings file exists', which an EMPTY
file satisfies. The property that actually matters is the opposite one: a NUMBER IN THE SOURCE
WITH NO CEILING BEHIND IT IS THE FAILURE. `MAX_EVENTS_PER_BATCH = 100` sat in the ingest route for
months naming no ceiling at all — and it was DOUBLE the documented Free per-invocation query limit.
Nothing could have told anyone, because there was no right-hand side to compare it to.
🔴 THE ONE RULE: A LIMIT WITHOUT A `source` IS NOT ENFORCED, IT IS REPORTED.
An invented ceiling fires on CORRECT input, which is strictly worse than no ceiling — the same
lesson tooling/ci/assert-store-metadata.mjs paid for when a made-up '120 characters or fewer'
rejected this repo's own 129-character fixture. So a row carrying a numeric `value` MUST carry a
`source` (an https URL) and a `verifiedOn` date, or the guard fails. A ceiling nobody could source
is written with `"value": null` and an `unverified` reason: it PRINTS on every run and CANNOT be
derived from. Marking something unverified is cheap and honest; inventing a number is neither.
Enforced by tooling/ci/assert-ceiling-budget.mjs:
· LIMB 1 every row with a numeric value has a `source` URL and a `verifiedOn` date      [B-6]
· LIMB 2 every `vendors.cloudflare.surfaces` entry in tooling/capability-register.json is
named by at least one ceiling row — a RELATIONSHIP to a list another guard already
maintains (assert-vendor-portability.mjs), so it cannot be shrunk to make this pass   [B-6]
· LIMB 3 every `const NAME = <number>` in services/*/src/ carries an `@ceiling` annotation:
either `@ceiling <id> lte` (and the guard CHECKS the arithmetic) or `@ceiling none — <reason>`.
An unannotated constant FAILS. A constant that exceeds its ceiling FAILS unless it declares
`@ceiling-exceeds <reason>`, which PRINTS on every run                                 [B-6]
· LIMB 4 every `.batch(` call site in services/*/src/ is named in `batchCallSites` with either
a bounding constant or an `unboundedReason` that PRINTS. A batch is the ONE construct that
turns one handler into N queries, so it is the shape queriesPerInvocation actually binds [B-6]
· LIMB 5 the deployed configs themselves: total cron triggers, distinct D1 database names,
distinct KV namespaces and every rate-limiter `period` are compared to their sourced
account-wide ceilings across services/*/wrangler.jsonc AND the brick template     [B-6, B-7]
⚠️ THE COVERAGE FLOOR IS A RELATIONSHIP, NOT A NUMBER. Limb 2's left-hand side is the vendor
surface list in tooling/capability-register.json; limb 3's domain is every numeric constant the
scan finds; limb 5's domain is every wrangler config on disk. There is no tuned integer to lower.
⚠️ NOT A PRICING FILE. These are PLATFORM LIMITS — the point at which a request is refused or a
write is rejected. Cost projections live in company/business/; they move independently and citing
one for the other is how a limit becomes a guess.

_why: Every ceiling below is recorded for the plan this portfolio actually runs on. Reading a PAID
number and deriving a cap from it would produce a Worker that is correct on a plan we do not
have — which is the failure mode that cannot be observed in CI at all, only in production.
planOfRecord.note: Cloudflare publishes Free and Paid side by side on the same pages. Where both exist, the row records the FREE value in `value` and the paid one in `paidValue`, so an upgrade is a one-line edit rather than a re-research.

ceilings.ambiguity: 🔴 UNRESOLVED, AND IT IS THE ARITHMETIC THAT MATTERS: the docs do NOT state whether a `D1Database.batch([s1..sN])` spends ONE query or N. The limits page states the 50 without qualifying batches; the Workers Binding API page for `batch()` describes it purely as a latency optimisation and never mentions a quota; the D1 pricing page mentions batches only for ROW counting. Neither reading can be cited. Every derivation from this row therefore takes the WORST-CASE reading — one statement = one query — because the other direction fails only in production, on the shared database every app depends on. Resolving it needs miniflare/`wrangler dev` against real D1 or a live probe; until then this sentence is the honest state and the caps below are conservative on purpose.
ceilings.note: Do NOT confuse this with the Workers subrequest limit. That is a separate, differently-sourced ceiling (workers.subrequestsToCloudflareServices, 1,000 on Free) and citing it as a rebuttal to the 50 is wrong: the 50 is D1-specific.

ceilings.ambiguity: None. The count is unambiguous and is checked against the deployed configs by limb 5.
ceilings.note: THIS is why an app's own backend is OPT-IN rather than the default ([ADR 020]). platform_db is one of the ten, so the portfolio can stand up NINE per-app databases on Free before the eleventh app is refused — and the brick's `{{app_id}}_db` means every backend stamp spends one.

ceilings.sourceText: Maximum database size: 10 GB (Workers Paid) / 500 MB (Free)
ceilings.ambiguity: None in the number. What IS unresolved is whether deleting rows RECLAIMS the space it counts — `cloudflare/workerd#1618` reports it does not, and the limits and pricing pages are both silent. That is [4]B-7's reclamation drill, not this row's business; recorded here so nobody derives a retention rule from this number believing deletion moves it.
ceilings.note: 500 MB × 10^6 is decimal, not 2^29. Recorded in BYTES so the comparison is exact; Cloudflare writes '500 MB' and this file takes the binary reading (500 × 1024 × 1024 = 524,288,000) deliberately, because it is the SMALLER of the two candidate values and a ceiling read too generously is a ceiling that does not bind.

ceilings.sourceText: Maximum storage per account: 1 TB (Workers Paid) / 5 GB (Free)
ceilings.note: 🔴 THIS IS THE CEILING THAT BINDS FIRST AT SCALE, and it is the arithmetic B-7 turns on. 5 GB across the whole account divided by a 50-app portfolio is ~100 MB per database — FIVE TIMES TIGHTER than the 500 MB per-database limit above. So splitting `events` onto its own database protects the per-database ceiling while doing nothing at all for this one; only a retention rule bounds this. That is exactly why the owner's 2026-07-27 decision was BOTH, and neither substitutes for the other.

ceilings.ambiguity: None. Stated once, with no plan split.
ceilings.note: The widest prepared statement in this repo binds 14 (`INSERT INTO events`, 14 columns), so there is 7× headroom. Recorded because the next hand-written multi-row `VALUES (?,?),(?,?)` INSERT is where this one bites, and it bites as a runtime error on a route that was passing.

ceilings.ambiguity: None in the number. `paidValue: null` here means UNLIMITED on paid, which is what the page says — it does not mean unsourced; a row is only treated as unsourced when `value` itself is null.
ceilings.note: Shared by EVERY app's launch path (config resolution) and every authenticated request (the JWKS warm cache). The 300s edge cache on GET /config/:app is what keeps this off the floor — but the query string is part of the cache key, so `?cb=<random>` misses deliberately and unboundedly. CONFIG_CEILING_LIMITER is the bound on that.

ceilings.sourceText: Writes to different keys: 1,000 writes per day (Free) / Unlimited (Paid)
ceilings.note: 🔴 THE TIGHT ONE, AND THE ONE A CACHE WARMER CAN EXHAUST. A JWKS cache that re-put on every miss rather than on every expiry would spend this in minutes under cold-isolate churn. JWKS_TTL_SECONDS is derived from this row for exactly that reason: at one write per TTL expiry, 600s gives at most 144 writes/day per namespace.

Not a real constraint at this portfolio's scale — recorded so that the SHARED-namespace design (one CONFIG_KV keyed `config:<app>`, one JWKS_CACHE) is a deliberate choice rather than a workaround for a limit nobody checked. The reason for sharing is operational, not quota-driven.

🔴 THE REASON [4]B-11 IS 'ONE CRON FOR THE PORTFOLIO'. Five triggers account-wide cannot be one-per-app at 50 apps; it cannot even be one-per-app at six. The consolidated 06:00 UTC scheduler with a per-app fan-out is not a tidiness preference, it is this number. Limb 5 counts the crons across every wrangler config in the repo, brick template included, so a stamped app that adds its own is caught at the stamp rather than at the account.

ceilings.sourceText: Accounts on the Workers Free plan have a daily request limit of 100,000 requests, resetting at midnight UTC. When a Worker exceeds this limit, Cloudflare returns Error 1027.
ceilings.ambiguity: None in the number. What the page does NOT settle is whether a scheduled (cron) invocation counts against it; it speaks of 'requests'. Treated as counting, because 2 invocations/day is noise either way and assuming otherwise would be an unsourced assumption in the expensive direction.
ceilings.note: The whole-portfolio ceiling every unauthenticated route shares. EVENTS_CEILING_LIMITER and CONFIG_CEILING_LIMITER exist because of this row: they are BURST bounds per (colo, asn), not accounting, so they narrow the funnel without ever proving this number is respected.

ceilings.sourceText: Request body size limits depend on your Cloudflare account plan, not your Workers plan. … Free: 100 MB … Requests exceeding these limits return a 413 Request entity too large error.
ceilings.ambiguity: None in the number. Note the page's own qualifier: this one tracks the CLOUDFLARE ZONE plan, not the Workers plan — the only ceiling in this file that does. Both are Free here, so the value is the same either way, but an upgrade of one does not move it.
ceilings.note: The OUTER bound on MAX_EVENTS_BODY_BYTES and MAX_CONSENT_BODY_BYTES. It is enormous relative to both (100 MB against 256 KiB), and that is the point: the edge would happily hand this Worker a 100 MB body, so the route's own byte ceiling is the only thing between an isolate and 100 MB of work it has already paid for. `surfaces: []` deliberately — this bounds the REQUEST, not any bound resource, so it contributes nothing to limb 2's coverage and must not appear to.

ceilings.sourceText: Workers on the free plan remain limited to 50 external subrequests and 1,000 subrequests to Cloudflare services per invocation.
ceilings.ambiguity: None in the number, but see the note — this row is here to be DISTINGUISHED from d1.queriesPerInvocation, not to be derived from.
ceilings.note: ⚠️ DO NOT DERIVE A D1 CAP FROM THIS. A D1 query IS a Cloudflare-service subrequest, so both ceilings apply and the SMALLER one binds: 50, not 1,000. Citing the 1,000 to justify a batch of 100 has been the wrong answer twice in this corpus, which is why the two rows sit next to each other with this sentence between them.

Binds the nightly scheduler's Supabase keep-alive fan-out: every project URL in SUPABASE_KEEPALIVE_URLS is one external `fetch`. At one identity project today this is nowhere near the limit; at 50 it would be the ceiling that stops the fan-out, not D1.

ceilings.ambiguity: None — this is an ENUMERATION, not a magnitude, which is why `value` is null and `allowedValues` carries the constraint. Limb 5 checks every deployed `simple.period` against it. A `period: 30` deploys and then behaves in a way nobody predicted.
ceilings.note: The set is the whole constraint. Cloudflare documents NO maximum on `limit` itself, so the three limiter magnitudes in services/platform/wrangler.jsonc (120/600/1200) are engineering choices reasoned in that file, NOT derivations from a published ceiling — and this register deliberately does not pretend otherwise.

ceilings.sourceText: permissive, eventually consistent, and intentionally designed to not be used as an accurate accounting system … For each unique key you pass to your rate limiting binding, there is a unique limit per Cloudflare location.
ceilings.ambiguity: UNVERIFIED BY CONSTRUCTION and it will stay that way — the vendor states there is no accurate number to have. `value: null` is correct here and is not a gap to be filled in later.
ceilings.note: 🔴 RECORDED AS A CEILING BECAUSE IT BOUNDS WHAT THE LIMITERS CAN CLAIM, not because it is a magnitude. The limit is PER CLOUDFLARE LOCATION, so a 600/min ceiling is 600/min at EACH colo — the account-wide daily budget (workers.requestsPerDay, d1.storagePerAccount) is NOT protected by any limiter here and needs the separate aggregate guard ([11]E-2). Anything that describes these three bindings as enforcing an account-wide budget is wrong, and this row is the citation for saying so.

_why: A `.batch([...])` is the ONE construct in this codebase that turns a single handler into N
queries — so it is the exact shape d1.queriesPerInvocation binds, and the only place the
worst-case reading of that row's ambiguity can actually bite. Every call site the scan finds
must appear here with either a `boundedBy` constant or an `unboundedReason` that PRINTS.
DERIVED, NOT DECLARED: the guard globs the call sites out of services/*/src/ and fails when it
finds one this block does not name, AND when this block names one the glob cannot find. A stale
entry is the same defect as a missing one — it makes the accounting look complete.

sites.note: One INSERT per well-formed event. This is the call site the 100 → 50 correction was about.

One DELETE plus one INSERT per category, deliberately in ONE batch so the replace is atomic. The bound is MAX_CATEGORIES + 1, and it currently exceeds the ceiling — see the `@ceiling-exceeds` declaration at the constant.
One UPSERT per entitlement id on a validated RevenueCat event.

sites.unboundedReason: The heartbeat writes ONE row per cron TARGET, and the target list is `appTargets()` — a compiled-in array in this repo, not caller input, so its size is a source edit and is visible in review. It is nonetheless unbounded in the arithmetic sense: at 50 apps this batch is 50 statements and crosses the Free ceiling under the worst-case reading. [4]B-11 (increment 9) is where the job/target set stops being a hardcoded array, and the chunking belongs with it rather than here, where it would be a second uncoordinated fan-out policy.

🔴 GENUINELY UNBOUNDED BY DATA, AND THE WORST OF THE FIVE. `ops` grows with the number of subscriptions due today PLUS one payment row per missed billing crossing, so a single app with a few hundred due renewals produces a batch far past 50 with no constant anywhere to annotate. It has never fired because Subly's row count is tiny. Chunking it is [4]B-11's increment (the fan-out already lives there) and must not be bolted on here: a retry/partial-failure policy invented at this call site would be the second one, and the cron's failure semantics are that increment's subject. Recorded, dated 2026-08-01, and printed on every run so it cannot go quiet again.

_why: Limb 5's inputs. Each names the ceiling row it compares against and the thing it counts across
every wrangler config in the repo — services/*/wrangler.jsonc AND the brick's service template,
because the brick is what multiplies any of these by the number of apps. assert-clone-contract
only ever inspects the throwaway CI probe stamp, which is exactly how a per-app R2 bucket stayed
live from 2026-07-17 with every guard green.

checks.counts: every entry of `triggers.crons`, summed across all configs
